sections.html:
Lancaster County covers about 846 square miles, with Lincoln as both the county seat and the state capital. Four cities lie inside it: Bennet, Hickman, Lincoln and Waverly. Villages include Davey, Denton, Firth, Hallam, Malcolm, Panama, Raymond, Roca and Sprague. A sale can involve a Lincoln house, an acreage near Branched Oak Lake or a village home in Hallam, and the same county offices process each of them.

The 2020 census counted 322,608 residents, 135,484 housing units and 5.6% vacancy. The homeowner vacancy rate was only 1.0 percent, so few owner-occupied homes sat empty. More than four in ten occupied homes were rented, which makes a house with a tenant in place a realistic situation for sellers here. The county is also heavily urban, with 90.3 percent of residents in urban areas, so most transactions involve city lots rather than farm ground.

sections.h2: Delinquent dates and where to pay
sections.html:
Lancaster County taxes are due December 31 each year. Because the county has more than 100,000 residents, Nebraska statute 77-204 makes the first half delinquent April 1 and the second half August 1. A first-half payment that would still be on time under a May 1 calendar is already late here.

Date or officeLancaster County detail
Taxes dueDecember 31
First half delinquentApril 1
Second half delinquentAugust 1
Walk-in office555 S. 10th Street, Room 102, Lincoln; Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Online search questions(402) 441-7425 or cotreasurer@lancaster.ne.gov

You can pay real estate and personal property taxes electronically through your bank or a bill payment service. The treasurer's property search shows each parcel's rate and tax district. Rates differ by district, so check the parcel you're selling instead of assuming a countywide rate. The treasurer collects for schools, fire districts, cities and villages alike.

Protests go to the County Clerk on Form 422 from June 1 through June 30 each year. Forms received before June 1 or postmarked after June 30 can't be accepted as timely.

The form must give the property description and the reason for the request, and the County Board of Equalization hears the protests. An unhappy outcome goes to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission within 30 days after the county board adjourns. The Assessor/Register of Deeds is a combined, elected office that supervises the assessment of all property in the county, phone (402) 441-8776.

Decisions on protests can continue well after the June window closes, but the filing window itself is only 30 days. Collect photographs, repair quotes and nearby sales before June 1.

Timing is the main thing to check, given the April 1 and August 1 dates. Three checks help:

  • Look up the parcel on the treasurer's property information search to see whether both halves of the prior year are paid.
  • Ask the closing agent whether the current-year bill will be paid in full from your proceeds or split with the buyer.
  • Confirm the mailing address on file, since statements follow the address given on the transfer statement filed with the deed.

The online figure is a starting point. Get a payoff in writing before closing.

Roofs matter too, since storms are a regular risk and buyers and insurers ask about them. Keep roof age and any prior claims handy.

Deeds are recorded at the Register of Deeds, 555 South 10th Street in Lincoln, for $10.00 on the first page and $6.00 for each added page. A deed must come with a completed Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, and the documentary stamp tax where it applies.

The office recommends emailing a copy to RegDeed@lancaster.ne.gov before mailing the original so staff can check recordability and fees. You can also record electronically through contracted vendors. The county adds no charge for e-filing, though each vendor sets its own fee. The office phone is 402-441-7463, and the staff can't complete documents or give legal advice.

The forms page includes the Certificate of Exemption for the documentary stamp tax (form 5b). The state rate is $3.32 per $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, and the seller pays it as grantor.

sections.h2: Selling a Lancaster County house for cash
sections.html: Owners with a tenant in place, a house needing repairs or a tight timeline sometimes compare a listing with a cash offer. Cash Home Buyers can review a Lancaster County address and explain how an as-is offer works. The title company confirms the tax payoff, prepares the deed and Form 521, and records it at the Register of Deeds. A cash sale skips showings, lender appraisals and repair negotiations, and you owe nothing if you decline.

faqs.q: When are Lancaster County property taxes delinquent?
faqs.a: The first half becomes delinquent April 1 and the second half August 1, under Nebraska statute 77-204, because the county has more than 100,000 residents.

faqs.q: What is the Lancaster County protest period?
faqs.a: Form 422 protests are accepted by the County Clerk from June 1 through June 30. Forms received before June 1 or postmarked after June 30 aren't timely.

faqs.q: Where is the Lancaster County treasurer's office?
faqs.a: The walk-in office is at 555 S. 10th Street, Room 102, Lincoln, open Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. You can also pay electronically through a bank bill payment service.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Lancaster County?
faqs.a: The filing fee is $10.00 for the first page and $6.00 for each additional page. You also need Form 521 and any documentary stamp tax, which is $3.32 per $1,000 of value on deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026.

faqs.q: Is the Lancaster County tax rate the same across the county?
faqs.a: No. Rates depend on the tax district, and the treasurer's property search shows the rate for each parcel.
